cards.title: Order ID and order-processing settings to configure at launch
cards.summary: Which Shopify general order settings to keep at default and how the order ID prefix/suffix helps hide store volume.
cards.use_when: Initial store setup or a settings audit for cart/checkout and fulfillment workflow before launch.
steps: Go to Settings > General > Orders in Shopify (verify current menu path in your admin, as Shopify's interface changes).

Use the order ID prefix/suffix field to add characters before or after order numbers — the source's purpose for this is to obscure how many orders you have actually received from customers who see the order number.
Keep 'require confirmation step' enabled. The source strongly recommends this: customers see an order summary before completing checkout, which reduces errors and unwanted orders.

Leave automatic fulfillment OFF for physical products, since most products have real fulfillment time; the source notes gift cards are the exception because Shopify emails them instantly and they need no fulfillment.

Auto-archive fulfilled orders is optional and depends on your workflow — the source says this is genuinely up to you, so decide based on whether you regularly revisit fulfilled orders for support or reporting.
Do not over-engineer this section; the source explicitly says order flow is 'not that big a thing' and you will find your own routine.
caveats: Settings labels and locations change between Shopify versions — confirm in your own admin.
Auto-fulfillment for non-gift-card products would mark orders shipped before they are, damaging delivery expectations.

cards.title: Configure Shopify customer notifications without breaking checkout emails
cards.summary: Which default Shopify notifications matter most, when each is triggered, and why you should barely edit the HTML.
cards.use_when: Notification and post-purchase communication setup for order confirmations, shipping updates and draft orders.
steps: Go to Settings > Notifications. The customer notifications are the most important group; the source prioritizes order confirmation and shipping confirmation above all others.

Order confirmation sends immediately when a customer orders and carries all order details. Keep customer email required at checkout — the source 'highly highly recommends' this, because if a customer only gave a phone number they may not receive the email confirmation and you would need SMS enabled instead.
Draft order invoice fires when you create orders manually in Shopify (draft orders).

Shipping confirmation fires automatically the moment a tracking number is added to an order — e.g. when a warehouse integration feeds tracking back into Shopify, Shopify emails the customer the tracking link with no action from you.
Other notifications exist (local pickup, local delivery, gift card, store credit); review them if relevant to your model but the source treats the first two as the priority.

If you edit an email, use the preview and send-a-test features. The source barely touches order confirmation — occasional small text or color changes only — because it must arrive with correct information. Deeper edits mean working in HTML code.
caveats: Timing and sending method are controlled by Shopify and cannot be changed — the source sees this as a benefit because it lowers error risk.
The source warns you can break these emails if you edit them without being sure what you are doing.

cards.title: Set up customer support before launch, not after
cards.summary: Staffing, tooling and policy choices that keep incoming order and shipping tickets from turning buyers into angry former customers.
cards.use_when: Preparing customer support capacity and response workflow ahead of a launch or high-volume sales period.
steps: Put a contact email or contact form on your contact page before launching — the source states you will receive customer emails as soon as the store goes live.
Answer each email quickly and effectively. The source warns that slow or poor replies turn customers and potential customers into angry people who dislike your brand.

At brand launch, keep support in-house — yourself, a family member or an employee — rather than outsourcing to a third-party support company. The source's stated reason is wanting full control early on.

Expect tickets about delivery, shipping and order status rather than product questions; if product pages are thorough, product questions should be rare. A detailed shipping policy reduces ticket volume but will not eliminate it.
Handle order changes in Shopify directly: you can open an order and edit fields such as the customer email, and fix addresses or change orders.

Use live chat for real-time contact — the source mentions a free Shopify chat app that works on mobile so you can reply from your phone. For large SKU catalogs needing tier-one help, consider an AI chat tool that answers first and escalates to a human; the source names Gorgias/Juie-style AI chat as an example. Verify current app names and pricing before committing.
Treat satisfaction as the mechanism for repeat purchase and brand durability, not as a nice-to-have.
caveats: The outsourced-support tradeoff is the source's opinion for early-stage brands only; larger operations may reasonably choose otherwise.
App names and free tiers change — verify before installing.

cards.title: Read conversion-rate funnel breakdowns to find where buyers drop
cards.summary: Using the Shopify conversion-rate breakdown to separate traffic, product-page, cart and checkout problems.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a weak conversion rate or deciding whether the problem sits in merchandising, PDP, cart or checkout.
steps: Open Analytics > Reports and locate the conversion-rate breakdown report, which shows the funnel stages: sessions, add-to-cart rate, reached-checkout rate and completed checkout (conversion rate).

Use the window and comparison settings deliberately — a single day's number is not your average conversion rate; pick a longer window (the source uses last 12 months and year-over-year comparisons) so the average is meaningful.
Locate the largest drop-off between adjacent stages rather than staring at the final number.

If the big gap is between add-to-cart and completed checkout, the source's example diagnosis is a shipping-rate problem pushing people away at checkout — investigate shipping cost presentation before rewriting product copy.
If add-to-cart itself is low, the issue is upstream: traffic quality or product page persuasion, not checkout.

Compare against your own historical baseline and niche, not a universal benchmark — the source calls 10% add-to-cart 'very good' and 2.63% completed conversion 'acceptable for our niche' as its own example, not a target.
When you know which stage leaks, at least one specific fix (shipping thresholds, PDP clarity, offer) can be tested instead of guessing.
caveats: The stated rates are the source's example store, not benchmarks to hit.
Shopify reports these metrics using its own definitions of gross vs net sales and session counting; check Shopify's documentation for current calculation methods.

cards.title: Choose the analytics time window and comparison before drawing conclusions
cards.summary: Why Shopify analytics require a long window and an explicit comparison period to mean anything.
cards.use_when: Any recurring analytics review, launch post-mortem or monthly performance meeting.
steps: In Analytics, set the time window first. Available options include today, yesterday, last 30 minutes, last 7 days, last 12 months, last week, year, weekday, month-to-date, quarter-to-date, year-to-date, plus a dedicated Black Friday/Cyber Monday section.

Use a long window for judgement calls: the source cautions that seeing 6% conversion today does not mean your average is 6%; you need 3, 6 or 12 months to see how the store actually performs and how it changed.
Optionally set a comparison window (e.g. previous year) when you want to see whether a strategy or change moved the business; the source sometimes turns comparison off because it can be confusing.
Set the display currency — useful if you sell in a currency other than your own and want to read your numbers in terms you understand.
Use live view for real-time behaviour during launches rather than for judging performance.
Expect the customer cohort/retention report and other data to be meaningless early — the source says you need roughly a year of customers, ads and sales before behaviour patterns are readable.
caveats: Short windows are for operational monitoring only, not for evaluating strategy.
Skip comparison when it makes the dashboard harder to read for your team.

cards.title: Customize the Shopify analytics dashboard around your own metrics
cards.summary: How to rearrange, add and save reports so the dashboard reflects what you actually manage.
cards.use_when: Setting up recurring reporting for a store you operate or manage, especially when the default dashboard hides the metrics you act on.
steps: From Analytics use the customize/edit control to drag and drop metric cards into the layout you want; the source describes this as easy drag-and-drop and recommends aligning it with your workflow and business.
Keep a default baseline view first so you understand Shopify's standard metric set before rearranging.

Go to Reports for topic-specific reporting: reports are grouped by category such as acquisition (sessions over time, visitors over time, sessions by social referrer), behaviour, customers, sales and finance.
Create your own reports and save them into the reports library — the source's example is a report comparing this year's sales to the previous year, saved for repeat access.
Filter reports by creator so you can find reports you or teammates built.
Use the sales reports' table/chart controls to change breakdowns when a chart alone is not answering the question.
Over time, let the dashboard evolve: the source frames the default setup as a starting point, not the destination.
caveats: Report names and category groupings are Interface-dependent — confirm available reports in your own admin.

Do not rearrange before you understand each metric's definition; the source stresses the difference between gross sales, discounts and net sales and points to Shopify's own documentation for how each is calculated.

cards.title: Use the customer cohort/retention report to time win-back emails
cards.summary: Reading retention month-by-month to learn when customers return and when to trigger reactivation.
cards.use_when: Planning retention and email reactivation timing for a store with at least several months of order history.
steps: Open the customer cohort analytics report from the analytics dashboard; it opens as a full report showing retention rate month after month over the selected window (the source looks at last 12 months).
Read two things: when returning customers come back, and what share of a cohort comes back in each period (e.g. of 100 customers acquired today, how many buy again in month 1, 2, 3, 6...).

Use that timing to schedule win-back emails: the source's example is that if customers typically return after four months, then customers who have not returned by four months should receive an email asking why, inviting them back and offering an incentive.
Use the pattern to estimate long-term customer value — how much revenue the same customer generates across a year or two — which informs how much you can spend to acquire them.
Expect the report to be uninformative before you have real data: the source says it only makes sense once you have roughly a year of ads, sales and collected customers behind you.
Treat this as the input for a retention calendar rather than a one-off read.
caveats: The four-month example is illustrative of the method, not a universal return cycle for your niche.
Small cohorts produce noisy retention percentages; wait for volume before acting aggressively.

cards.title: Ask Shopify's AI agent for custom analytics reports
cards.summary: Using Shopify's built-in AI exploration and Sidekick to generate reports without building them manually.
cards.use_when: Producing a quick custom report (e.g. multi-year conversion trend) without manually constructing charts in the reports library.
steps: Access the AI report tool from Shopify analytics via the new exploration option; the source also references Sidekick, Shopify's AI agent, for analytics, reports and other store help.
State the report you want in plain language — the source's example prompt is a report showing conversion-rate improvement over the last two years.
Review the query the tool writes and the resulting report; the source notes the tool composed the query itself in its simple example.

Use it for analysis and report generation, not as a replacement for understanding metric definitions — the source still directs you to Shopify's documentation for how gross vs net sales and similar figures are calculated.
Keep any report you will reuse (save it into the reports library) so you are not re-prompting each period.
caveats: The source calls its demo prompt a very basic example; complex questions may need refinement.
AI features and their availability change quickly — verify the current entry point and capabilities in your Shopify admin.

cards.title: Read the sales breakdown and by-channel metrics correctly
cards.summary: Interpreting gross sales, net sales, discounts, channel attribution and AOV before acting on them.
cards.use_when: Monthly performance review, channel-mix decisions or pricing/discount evaluation.
steps: Start with the dashboard summary cards: gross sales, returning customer rate, orders fulfilled and total orders — the source treats returning customer rate as a headline health metric alongside revenue.

Open the total sales breakdown and learn the difference between gross sales and net sales, and how discounts sit between them. The source stresses this explicitly and points to Shopify's own resources for the exact calculation of each figure.

Check total sales by sales channel to see where revenue actually originates, and use acquisition reports such as sessions by social referrer to see where visits come from — revenue channel and traffic channel are separate questions.
Track average order value over time as its own trend line; the source calls AOV a very important metric.
Check total sales per product to identify best sellers and confirm whether your catalog bets are paying off.
Read total sales over time month to month to spot improvement or decline in context of the window and comparison you set.
caveats: Metric definitions are Shopify's, not universal — always confirm the calculation before comparing to external benchmarks.
Channel attribution in Shopify reflects Shopify's own channel labelling; a channel with high sessions may contribute little revenue.

cards.title: Don't rely on default Shopify emails to fix weak product pages
cards.summary: Using post-purchase and support signals to detect product-page and policy gaps rather than patching them with notifications.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to expand shipping policies, FAQ content or PDP copy after launch based on incoming support tickets.
steps: Use the source's stated expectation as a diagnostic: if product pages are thorough, customers should mostly not be asking product questions; most tickets will be about delivery, shipping or order status.
Classify incoming tickets into product questions versus logistics questions for the first weeks after launch.
A high volume of product questions indicates weak PDP content or missing sizing/spec/usage information — fix the page rather than answering the same question repeatedly.
A high volume of shipping/delivery questions indicates weak shipping-policy detail — the source states a very detailed shipping policy reduces ticket volume, though it will not eliminate it entirely.

Resist changing order-confirmation and shipping-confirmation emails (which are order-status communications) as a substitute for fixing pre-purchase clarity; the source keeps those emails essentially untouched.
Handle genuine per-order requests (email change, address fix, order modification) individually in Shopify instead of treating them as content problems.
caveats: Even a strong PDP will not stop all contacts; the source accepts individual order-change requests as normal.
This is the source's stated expectation based on its experience, not a measured benchmark.

From your Shopify dashboard, when you go to settings under the general settings, there is a part related to orders. And in this part, you have first the order ID and the order processing. So for the order ID, this is basically you adding a like an extension before the order number or after the order number in order for your customers like to hide the number of orders that you have received. I think I've covered this. The second part is the order processing part and this is where you can modify some settings related to the how you process the orders. So for example in the first option you can make the confirmation step required. I highly recommend you to keep this. So basically your customers are going to see a summary of their order before checking out. The second thing is to automatically fulfill orders. Also I don't recommend you to change the settings.

 For gift cards you can automatically uh fulfill them because Shopify is going to send the gift card by email. So there is no fulfillment time but for the other products most probably you will have fulfillment times. So keep this as it is. And the final one is to automatically archive the order once it is uh fulfilled. It's also up to you and your workflow. You can keep it or remove it. It's really up to you. The second thing I want to talk about are the notifications and those are very important because they are part of your communication with your customers and they have are sent by default from Shopify. So you can't uh change the timing of of sending them. You can't affect how to send them. Shopify is going to take care of them totally which is actually nice because it lowers the error possibility margins let's say. So from your settings you go to notifications and as you can see you have several ones. First you have the customer notifications and those are the most important ones. So you have first the order confirmation, the draft order invoice, the shipping confirmation. So the order order confirmation is going to be sent directly when someone makes an order. They will receive this email uh on their inbox with all the information. If you allowed your customers at the checkout to give their phone number or their email, they might not be receiving the order confirmation by email. So in this case, you need to activate SMS. And that's why I highly highly recommend you to keep the email required at the checkout uh page for the um for the for the order. If you click in here on the order confirmation, you will have a preview. You will see a preview of the email. So as you can see, this is the email and this is the SMS if you want to uh activate it. I highly recommend you not to touch this email if you are not like 100% sure of what you are doing. Personally, I barely touch this email. I might change the text a little bit. I sometimes change the color, stuff like that, but nothing else because it's a very important email and I want to make sure my customers received it with the right information. After you do your changes, you can send a test if you wish a test email and preview it on your inbox. After the order confirmation, you have the draft order invoice.
